translations.title: How Shall I Name You?
translations.text:
How shall I name you

when I think of you

and you are not here:


my wild strawberry

my candied lizard

my comfort cone

my silk spinner

cuckoo of my cares

my Aurelia

my gravel flower

my dream creature

my morning hand

my great forgetter

cruiser of my window

my moon concealer

my silver crook

my evening dusk

my solar thread

my snub-nosed hare

my deer head

my hare's paw

my stair frog

my garland of lights

my spring thief

my trembling nag

my silver snail

my inkwell

my brush-tailed fox

my woodcutter

my stormy fugitive

my bear keeper

my tooth-bearer

my horse's ear

my tree in the Prater

my spiral horn

my monkey carrier

my end of winter

my artichoke

my midnight

my countdown


(From the top!)
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Outside the Pine, the Gray Fir, the Rainy Pine of Flanders...
translations.text:
Outside, the pine, the gray fir, the rainy pine of Flanders

and the talk in the inn's summerhouse

with that scent of beer


in the morning, toward the gray cloud heights
a window opens there so early
wide open, like air flowing apart
arms stretch out, opening the windows


on the far side of the day, the fall
of gray melancholy
these dusks gray as dust
disappearing with trains and mists, breaking through again:
beneath them, Vineta, city of bells.


And then the night
black, as if one's hand were in water up to the wrist
we stumble toward the door:
oh, so many stars
and a black lock across the face
barefoot on the creaking stairs.

The moths fluttering:
frightened house swallows like bats and will-o'-the-wisps
and the horrible honey tongue of dead flies.


Now
in the midst of spring, submerged
after many months:
an open purse
an old cigarette from the Rue des Dames
a little bag of soda
a piece of hardened bread
on the bed, the mold of your body.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Piggyback
translations.text:
‘Piggyback,’ said my cousin, while

barberized, barberized, barberized

he walked along our street

with a little suitcase under his arm

and still feeling widowed

from the companion of his life

the other funeral guests had come too

the double cast of mourners

with lingerie crepe over rose-colored lips

but he passed me with a dissolving face

and greeted me like someone

who, just as so many times before,

takes upon himself once more

the world's great surge

in his little boat of solitude.


Now then, dear ants, how are you?

Do you like being here in this flourishing land?

You never rest, for what suits you best is

to swarm according to the plan whispered to you

violet faces, round heads, doll eyes

Roman cut on a fine blond cranial type

lying down with Schubert songs, listening on the plush ramp

strawberry cheeks

turn around completely so

your whole figure can be seen

turn back, live; a smile is not enough

a glance emerging from behind the shop windows

or the tender touch of two eyes set far apart

but you must head

toward the dance, temptation, entanglement

you will go on step by step

or stop and stand motionless:

someone will always come to help you out

of the fix

but it takes a long time to realize

what should have happened and what did happen

then one stops again and holds one's breath

or hums a song or

begins to love jazz.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Love and Appetite
translations.text:
Well said, Schlosser: one loves
what is one's own; and if one has none,
one desires it. The rich soul
loves; the poor one desires.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Immortal Remembrance
translations.text:
Tell me, my friend, the cause of this ardent,
pure, immortal longing within me:
to hang upon your lips forever,
and drown in your being, and receive
the sweet air of your immaculate soul.


In time gone by, in another time,
was not our existence one being?
Did the heart of an extinct planet
give our love a nest in its depths
in days we saw flee forever?


…You too, like me? Yes, you have felt
in your breast the sweetest beating
with which passion announces its fire:
let us love each other, and soon, happy,
we shall take flight to that heaven
where once again we shall be as God.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Three Lessons I Would Trace...
translations.text:
I

I would trace three lessons
with a burning pen that scorched deeply,
leaving a trail of blessed light
wherever a mortal heart beats.


II

Have Hope. If there are storm clouds,
if there are disappointments and no illusions,
unfurrow your brow; its shadow is vain,
for every night is followed by a morning.


III

Have Faith. Wherever your boat is driven
by roaring breezes or raging waves,
God (do not forget) rules heaven,
and earth, and breezes, and the little boat.


IV

Have Love, and love not just one being,
for we are brothers from pole to pole,
and spend your love for everyone's good,
as the sun pours out its friendly light.


V

Grow, love, hope! Engrave the three within you,
and wait firm and serene
for strength where others may founder,
light when many wander in darkness.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ecstasy for Laura
translations.text:
Laura, if your tender gaze
sinks its flashing ray into mine,
my happy spirit, born anew,
slides in a blazing gust
with May's sunlight.
And if I gaze into your peaceful eyes
without shadows or veils,
I breathe, enraptured,
the airs of heaven.


If your lip gives its sonorous note
to the air with a sigh,
and the sweet harmony
of golden stars,
I hear the angels' choir,
and my soul, transfixed,
finds ecstasy in lucid love.


If in the harmonious dance
your foot glides like a timid wave,
I watch the mysterious troop of loves
stir their wings;
the tree moves its branches behind you
as if Orpheus' lyre were sounding,
and the earth we tread beneath my feet
spins dizzyingly.


If the pure gleam of your eyes
kindles love's fire,
it gives a heartbeat to hard marble
and calls life into the barren trunk.
All the joy imagination dreamed
I now behold, present and certain,
when I read in your eyes, my Laura!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: The Maiden's Lament
translations.text:
The clouds quickly gather,
the forest oaks roar;
a maiden sits
beside the green bank.
The waves break in fury;
she sighs in the darkening night,
and laments with eyelids drowned in tears:


My heart is dead within me,
the world is empty;
desire has abandoned me,
every hope is destroyed.
I have tasted the fullness of happiness,
I have lived, I have loved;
take now this sacred child
into your tender keeping.


Your grief is vain,
in vain your tears fall;
for the dead in their beds
never remember their dreams.
Even if something could soothe your sorrow,
pour sweet balm through your veins,
now that love and its pleasures no longer bind you,
cry out your desire, and find comfort in silence!


Though my grief be in vain,
though my tears fall in vain;
though the dead can remember
nothing of their dreams;
no balm is sweet to an abandoned heart,
when love and its pleasures no longer bind us;
only misery and lonely torment remain.




“Des Mädchens Klage”
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: The Division of the Earth
translations.text:
“Take the earth!” from his high throne
said He who filled the void to men.
“To fulfill my sovereign purpose,
divide it among yourselves as brothers;
I give it to you as inheritance and domain.”


Each mortal hurried to answer the call,
each came first as best he could,
and took for his own all he could command: 
the earth's fruits, the farmer;
the forest where the knight would hunt.


The merchant fills his barn and chest;
the monk takes the shadowed vineyard;
and the king, feeling strong at last,
marks roads and bridges off with barriers,
saying: “The tithe! The tithe is mine.”


Years later, when at last the irrevocable
division had been completed,
the poet came from a distant land.
Alas! Every field was bounded,
and every thing subject to its lord.


“Too late, in vain I ask my share!
Have you left the most faithful one in misery,
O God, and disinherited your son?”
Thus the poor bard said in tears,
prostrate before his Lord's throne.


“If, lost in the region of dreams,”
God answered, “you delayed, deluded one,
do not weep in vain or accuse me:
where were you, expecting me to forget you?”
“Where? At your side!” replied the dreamer.


My eyes were nourished by your beauty,
my ears by heaven's harmonies;
if I scorned earthly things on high,
it was your glory, shining without peer,
that held my mind and senses captive!


And God: “What can I do? On earth
nothing remains to fulfill your longing;
the forest and nearby estate are another's…
Come with me to heaven, if you please;
from today I shall freely admit you!”
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Technocrat Ballad
translations.text:
Memento at the San Isidro fair



Little heart, scarcely elegiac, weary of science

the sad books unread, the ambiguous prayers

embarked without a wristwatch, ignorant of the stars

weary of wisdom, the astrolabe is a nominative.



Movement too is weary and dragged out

metronomic because it is number, not name

the train crosses the bridge and then falls.



Little of a night owl, yet disoriented and afflicted

by confusion tangled in irregular actions

the verbs, the pronouns punished facing the wall.

Entirely kind.



Ash of all the ashes, enamored ash:

the priapic, gagged and dry, trembling

to make an amulet of it, tell friends about it

to leap from the top floor.

















Whistling her tune to the left

with the train beneath her peach-shaped buttocks

a tooth still piercing her breast

and her leg's disdain for the nylon stocking

on the way to airing out a love affair

she plunges into the sea and orders two horchatas

toasting the air: “Cheers, cheers!”

the burnished athlete then approaches

“I know what's happening, and your Weltanschauung—

your willfulness, I mean;

he, by contrast—plagiarizing Scott Fitzgerald—

is scholastic even when buying tobacco.”

She cries out joyfully and smiles

at night, and in intimate union the two urinate

and sing in duet:

“Nothing is as clear as the human sciences,

nothing as Taylorist as psychiatry.”
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: This, Whom You Hail Aloud (O Bulequino!)
translations.text:
This man, whom you loudly acclaim (O Bulequino!)
as John of Austria, in a prominent
august city: a young man exalted
(if humane to all) is divine.


Maborte girded him with fine steel,
his victorious, all-powerful sword;
let Flanders say it, let it speak eloquently,
let Parthenope and Barcelona say it.


Today, clothed in peace and glory,
we see him as peerless arbiter
of Justice in all contingencies.


O Buluquino, you who travel the world
observing all its wonders:
since there is nothing more to see, take no more steps.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Celia, Blame Your Error, Not Your Harm
translations.text:
Celia, blame your error, not your harm;
nature made you one alone.
Tell me, then, why does your beauty wish
to give you a second self by such a new deceit?


No, the mirror did not break, and I wonder
that your gaze should miss its wholeness;
it was only glass; now, after disillusion,
it begins to be a mirror.


Your portrait, divided among portraits,
dies in one part, in another it achieves
a fuller means of deserving you.


Here my error stands more clearly warned,
for when you wound my hope most deeply,
my desire, an immortal Hydra, is reborn.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Divine Phoenix in a Mortal Dawn
translations.text:
Divine phoenix, in a mortal dawn
your tomb dissolves into light,
and your beauty, inheriting itself,
mocks our grief and your decline.


Funeral pomp and tears deceive,
for your being was not in your form:
nothing lives in what merely lasts,
nor need an accident die.


Your realm has failed, Love, your nest
in Amarilis; yet afterward you persist
in wielding your cruelties through their effects.


O never-heard-of way of killing!
When Love sees itself free of tyrannies,
it begins to kill us with mercy!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Nature's Credit
translations.text:
Your dawn was nature's credit,
for it trusts its splendor to you;
your death, a providence that feared
to exhaust its gifts in your abundance.


Your Fame wins a more immortal laurel
for your head than your Monarchy: 
the latter ended on your fateful day,
the former forever begins to crown you.


You are a great exception to oblivion,
honor of Macedonia, whose name alone
achieved all that one world can hold.


To give you to us, you died, grateful
to the gods; you were their envy,
for then Rome believed you were a man.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: She Flees Through Mines of Crystal and Scarlet
translations.text:
Through mines of crystal and scarlet
in Finea flows a steady flood;
a stone that rejects its native moisture
to remain more stone, more tyrant.


The frozen flint, when struck, pours out
living sparks that feign it lives.
Finea weeps; the sensitive fluid lies
if ever it has treated her as human.


In love's storm, love surges,
and blind in water, lightning, sighs,
repeats a thousand trials of one death.


Your tears are fire, Finea.
In a storm where water is fire,
death is a brief effect of lightning.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: From the Last Sleep in Which I Lay
translations.text:
From the final sleep in which he lay,
the solicitous lover was mocked
by Anaxarete, watching snow steal
its last cold rose.


She, always rebellious, dismissed
not hardness but her fierce soul,
and gave hatred an alabaster fortress,
for she loathed her flesh for being soft.


You can be no harder now, Lisi,
and though some punishment awaits you,
it will be to take form in my tender love.


You will be more immortal in my pure faith,
for I pledge myself to your hardness,
than in hateful marble, though it be eternal.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: That Clock a Sovereign Hand
translations.text:
That clock, which a sovereign hand
sealed as a sign, though it was a gift,
and made the benefit more binding than law,
sparing the clamor of a bell;


that chain which, in no vain workmanship,
halts Time in his revolving task,
reducing him to eternal sacrifice
(due pomp for one who rose beyond the human):


it is a great honor, a shining atom,
of Leonor's ingenious sun,
which spreads to Spain from Hungary,


that but one life was allotted to you,
short, Fabio, beside so weighty a favor,
and grants you time in which to be grateful.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: From What Infernal Depth...
translations.text:
From what infernal depth, whose fire,
infamous, opposes you to the glorious?
Sweet in origin, poisonous in effect,
I worship and condemn you myself.


Only this is true in you, full of horrors: 
the torment, the lying object.
What greater signs of treachery
than poison always equivocal?


No wonder, if proud Alcides,
Jove made human, adopted by heaven,
now rages for you, now dies weakened.


Scornfully he overcame; in love he yielded;
only to jealousy did he confess his mortality;
Deianira gave him a shroud while he lived.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: What Does It Matter That Etna Is Snow-Covered...
translations.text:
What does it matter that Etna is snow-covered
if its entrails burn with hidden fire?
What love boasts of
it finds lacking in what is revered.


The rose is harder in the meadow's commonwealth
when the gardener discovers it too late
than the one warned to guard herself
by the plow's first experience.


Beauty lasts not a single moment
longer than desire, and desire lies
as soon as experience has passed.


So says vigilant modesty: 
it is misfortune to die by accident,
and folly to die by design.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: This Divided Image of Life
translations.text:
This divided image of life,
a shining clock or numbered light,
which describes it as easily as a rose,
interrupted by a breath, a moment's calm;


this flame, fading before the sun,
seems more a butterfly than a flame;
this fatal sphere, so severe,
each moment of it a murderer:


it is, Fabio, a double lesson. Do not resist
disillusion with your fragile fate: 
time and beauty have their limits.


The ordered motion of the spheres
is a sundial, and warns the sun
that what lasts longest is mortal too.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: What Deceits, Celia, What Follies...
translations.text:
What deceits, Celia, what follies are stirred
by blind error, madder than blindness,
if while I compete with fire
you study how to outdo white snow;


if you give wandering gold to the light breeze,
while I surrender my freedom to its error,
or then compete with the wanton vine,
reducing it to so many little rings?


Beware lest the harsh serpent of future age
break the one you have now,
before you lose the fruit of your April.


Would you not laugh at spring
if with useless pomp it denied us fruit
to enjoy the flowers forever?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Now Dust Is Not Ruin, but Breath
translations.text:
Now dust is not ruin but breath;
now the immortal entrusts itself to mortal.
Here daring reached its aim
and intention carved its ideas.


Prudent, it chooses clay for its instrument,
seeking a form proportionate to its daring;
intending to give it spirit,
it attributed the human to its element.


Now that eternity has breathed into the figure,
where the Sun of Iberia will be born again,
the Andalusian Lysippus entrusts it to clay.


Bronze and marble might claim the reverence
of years, for their solid substance,
but Philip alone suffices for eternity.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Like a Sick Man Longing on a Burning Bed
translations.text:
Like a sick man longing, on a burning bed,
to recover through excess,
whose self-deception or stubbornness alone
brings relief as the illness grows;


and like the deer that feels the arrow,
fleeing itself in vain by night and day,
to see if healing waters might offer
cool flattery from a temperate spring;


so, love's slave, with wounded breast,
I sought a remedy in absence;
I sought a spring against the elusive dart.


Then Love, against my will, did
what excess does in sickness
and a master with a fugitive slave.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: It Is Written in Rome, I Have Noticed
translations.text:
It is written in Rome, I have noticed—
and I marveled, an incredulous witness—
that whoever reaches greatest intimacy with a friend
should keep part of his heart in reserve;


for if fate should reduce him
to suffer that friend's ingratitude or enmity,
it was judgment—or vengeance—to find within himself
a stronghold untouched by the fire.


Ignacio, then, friend and wise man,
this happy age now brings you to us;
to your discretion we appeal with our doubt.


Which should we fear as the greater injury:
the noble death of trust,
or the shameful safety of caution?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: I Beg You, Lisi, That You Enjoy Your Blooming Age
translations.text:
I begged you, Lisi, to enjoy your blooming age
before this frozen age arrived;
you scorned my warning, and surrendered,
I see you regret the harm too late.


In old age, which comes unrecognized,
you feel two losses: in the years gone by
you did not enjoy beauty, disillusioned,
and now you do not enjoy the form you sought.


When remedy was possible, your ambition
did not recognize the harm; now you know
no remedy for harm discovered too late.


Yet, remembering the old deception,
I shall watch you, enjoying these hours,
not what I want, but what I once wanted.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: O You Who Silently Prescribe the Beloved Dust
translations.text:
O you who silently prescribe
the beloved dust, hard source of my tears,
since death grants you such authority,
how you know my praise, how you feel;


tell Lisi of my love; her holy fate
no longer allows unjust disdain.
Let your nature, marble, lose whatever
your hardness feigns of her disdain;


join our ashes; let death win here
a new triumph over life: 
admit me at last, the effect of her eyes.


If, only because of your grim silence,
the form of my slayer was entrusted to you,
how much more do my remains deserve?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Let the Confusion of Repeated Deceit Cease
translations.text:
Let the confusion of repeated deceit cease,
O Fabio, and let its horrors no longer trouble
the divine splendors of truth
that my forgetfulness profaned.


Experience enlightens the senses;
what I judged favor is now danger;
I see my errors clearly
and mourn the time I wasted.


Let disillusion be a sure north star
in the fierce waves I sail,
for grateful wisdom adores its lesson.


Let someone blinder sail the stormy sea;
he is no wise man who, from one same harm,
weeps his mistakes a second time.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Now, From Sheer Pain, I Feel No Pain
translations.text:
Now, from sheer pain, I feel no pain;
my care has become my nature,
and I am so used to suffering
that joy frightens me more than torment.


Disdain is enough, and thought alone
to destroy a loving heart;
who waits to die of being scorned
finds his own feeling merciful.


Love dies and is reborn in a pair of eyes
more often than the sun sees its light,
now alive in gold, now tinged with shadow.


But, ah, Love, I excuse your anger: 
if you give me death in order to live,
I ask, why must you give me life?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Sceva, After the Final Wound
translations.text:
Sceva, after the final wound
that sealed his fame,
sold his death and thus his sword,
having bought his glory with his life.


“Is there no one,” he cried, “to carry
news of my fall to my eager foe?
I feel that dying while doing nothing is pointless;
let me matter, dead or as a killer.”


He spoke, and a trusting soldier seized him,
when Sceva spent the breath with which he was dying
to kill the daring man,


saying: “I shall die, but avenged
for the insult of this man who thought
that even dying he could see me overcome.”
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: To the Wind He Entrusted His Hope and Striving
translations.text:
To the wind he entrusted hope and striving,
as Apollo pursued Daphne;
the fear that hastened her steps
clothed her white foot in wings.


The wind turned the gold of her tresses
into rays with which she shot at the Sun,
while unjust Love prepared
the greatest victory for the one who fled;


then the nymph cried to her flowing father,
and, made human as a laurel, found revenge
on the Sun through Peneus's aid.


“Alas,” Apollo said to the disdainful tree,
“why, if my hope perishes in you,
do you offer desire a green likeness?”

translations.title: In Living Waves of Wounded Scarlet
translations.text:
In living waves of wounded scarlet
Lisi's sought-for wound breaks open.
She feels the lost purple less
than finding herself already human.


She remained like a rose that died too soon,
warned too late that it would fade,
whom the wind struck down in life
without letting her learn vanity's lesson.


Pale, Lisi, your face appears.
Never is lightning more rightly feared
than when the sky turns pale.


Let Love consider, for whom you triumph
in the feigned death of a faint: 
what will she do alive, who kills as she dies?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Speak, Animated Figure, Let Not Your Silence
translations.text:
Speak, animated figure; let not your evasive
silence offend your modern father;
let me speak, so it may be clear
which is painted and which alive.


You do not feel, nor do I, though I live
to give my pain its ill-starred reins.
You are silent, and so am I, though I burn
with a fire in which I die and come to be.


Your figure knows nothing of my figure;
you offer a steadfast face, not by chance,
for you portray my contrary fate.


O power of Love, to make now
another self to suffer what I suffer,
denied the relief of death!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: These Are Leisure Hours from a Labor I Wrote
translations.text:
These are leisure hours from a labor I wrote
in a rough age with an untuned reed;
a device of Love, who condemns to this
the one who hated moderation.


I sang of pain, weeping for joy,
and sometimes sang my grief so sweetly
that everyone thought it belonged to another,
but my soul knows well that it was mine.


If you are not celebrated by everyone,
voices of love, look at my thoughts:
you will see no better fortune awaits you.


Let no discerning soul call you wasted,
for if the wind alone carries you away,
there you will meet my hope.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Until You Die, Brave Youth
translations.text:
Until you die, brave youth,
dying and surrendering were one thing;
now there will be two, for the first corpse
dies yet does not rest.


You alone, after your setting,
leave Death, attentive and dutiful,
so suspended that she wonders, afraid,
whether you or she suffers the stroke.


Whose courage, I ask, lasted longer than life?
Who deserved death?
Or was he envied as uncertain dust?


O unheard-of foresight of fate,
which reserves you for this new matter: 
to be immortal after you are dead!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Today, Noroña, the Bloody King of Beasts
translations.text:
Today, Noroña, the bloody king of beasts
confounds his ruin with his glory.
The blow would not have cost you victory
if you had divided the feint from the blow.


You await a reward beyond desire,
renewing Hercules' story today.
What will the victor's memory be
if the heavens honor the trophy?


Fix the beast's hide upon the sky's,
and your glory will take new life;
let Olympus owe Spain a new sign.


It is no accident it rises to such flight,
for unless borne up to heaven
such a feat could not fit within the world.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Stranger, He Does Not Lie Here, Sternly Absent
translations.text:
Stranger, he does not lie here; sternly absent
is the man whose most learned experience
left even Apollo, who gave him knowledge,
first only in time.


So that death's rule might endure,
incompatible now with his presence,
he departed; the sentence would not have been fulfilled
had he not sided with his own steel.


Not in human health, which deceives time,
but in life that time could not end,
he could halt his enlightened thought.


Let us mourn, then, envious of his passing,
for he first fashioned what would leave us
without health for all, and life for himself.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Seeing Spain's Early Loss
translations.text:
Seeing the early loss of Charles,
who now adds to the stars,
Spain laments before a mindful goddess
who dwells proudly in an immortal temple.


Divine in knowledge and human in answer,
she nourishes Spain not with comfort alone,
but in glorious rapture presents her
to Charles, who makes her complaint vain.


Her complaints are overcome and satisfied;
her tears now spring from joy,
as she beholds a Christian Gothic army.


She sees Charles among beautiful forms,
added to his noble ancestors;
she departs joyful, consoling her great brother.
